pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Protecting Eyes from Sunlight

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 3 Science, Light):** recognise that light from the sun can be dangerous and that there are ways to protect their eyes. (Non-statutory guidance: pupils should be warned that it is not safe to look directly at the sun, even when wearing dark glasses.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No NGSS performance expectation covers sun/eye safety — this is a UK-specific health-and-safety objective rather than a physics PE; in US schemes it sits under health/safety education, not the NGSS waves strand. (NGSS waves PEs concern how light behaves, e.g. 1-PS4-2/3, not eye safety.)

- **Operational details:** The load-bearing message is a non-negotiable safety RULE plus its reason. Lead by eliciting and explicitly challenging the dominant misconception — that it is safe to look at the Sun if it is cloudy or if you are wearing sunglasses — and correct it directly: NEVER look straight at the Sun, even with dark glasses. Give an age-appropriate why: the eye's lens focuses sunlight to a point on the retina (like a magnifying glass), which can burn the light-sensitive cells, and instruments (binoculars/telescopes) make it far worse. Separate EYE protection (sunglasses for general brightness/UV; never staring at the Sun; safe indirect viewing via a pinhole projector) from SKIN protection (sunscreen, clothing, shade). UV beads support a fair test of which sunglasses block the most UV — useful evidence for 'ways to protect', but reinforce that blocking UV is NOT the same as making it safe to stare. Model accurate language (the Sun APPEARS to move) to avoid seeding astronomy misconceptions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 7–8 success is stating the rule (never look at the Sun, even with sunglasses, even when cloudy), giving a simple reason (it can damage the eyes), and naming ways to protect eyes (and, distinctly, skin). This is safety knowledge plus a simple cause; the optics of focusing/retinal detail is teacher background, not a pupil expectation.
bestPractices: Lead by eliciting then explicitly refuting the key misconception that the Sun is safe to look at when cloudy or through sunglasses — the rule is NEVER look directly at the Sun, even with dark glasses.
Give an age-appropriate reason (the eye focuses sunlight onto the retina and can burn it; instruments make it worse) so the rule is understood, not just imposed.
Distinguish eye protection (sunglasses, never staring, safe indirect viewing) from skin protection (sunscreen, clothing, shade) — they are different needs.
Use UV-sensitive beads to fair-test which sunglasses/sun creams block the most UV — hands-on evidence for 'ways to protect' — while stressing that blocking UV ≠ safe to look at the Sun.
Provide a safe indirect way to observe the Sun (pinhole/box projector) rather than ever direct viewing.
Model accurate language ('the Sun appears to move across the sky') to avoid reinforcing Sun/Earth astronomy misconceptions; reinforce that all skin tones need UV protection.
keyRepresentations: A clear 'NEVER look at the Sun — even with sunglasses' rule card
A simple eye diagram: sunlight focused by the lens onto the retina (why it harms)
UV-sensitive beads used to fair-test different sunglasses / sun creams
A pinhole / box projector for safe indirect Sun viewing
An eye-protection vs skin-protection sorting display
commonMisconceptions: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day (cloud removes the danger).
Wearing sunglasses (or 'dark enough' glasses) makes it safe to look directly at the Sun.
The Sun is only dangerous on hot/bright summer days.
If it doesn't feel hot or look painfully bright, the Sun isn't harmful to the eyes.
Only some skin tones need protection from UV, rather than everyone.
Sunglasses protect the eyes the same way for staring as for general brightness (conflating UV protection with safe direct viewing).

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, teach the non-negotiable safety rule that you must NEVER look directly at the Sun — even through sunglasses, even on a cloudy day — paired with a simple, age-appropriate reason (the Sun is so bright it can permanently damage the light-sensitive cells inside the eye). Lead by surfacing then directly refuting the central misconception that sunglasses or cloud make it safe to stare. Separately build the 'ways to protect' half of the objective: naming eye protections (sunglasses for general brightness/glare, shade, hat, and safe indirect viewing via a pinhole/box projector) distinct from skin protections (sunscreen, clothing, shade, hat), and optionally testing which sunglasses block the most UV using UV-sensitive beads — while stressing that blocking UV is not the same as making direct viewing safe. The focusing/retinal optics is teacher background; the pupil expectation is the rule, a simple cause, and named protections.

activities.title: The Sun-and-eye safety scene: naming the 'but I've got sunglasses' excuse
feedback: If a learner says sunglasses make staring safe: sunglasses reduce glare for comfort and block some UV, but they never make direct Sun-gazing safe — the safe move is not to look at all.
If a learner says a cloudy or dim-looking Sun is safe to view: don't judge safety by how bright it happens to look; the Sun is still dangerously intense through thin cloud or haze.
Affirm the pinhole/box projector answer: watching the projected image of the Sun on a surface lets you observe it without ever pointing your eyes at the Sun.
activities.rationale: Fixed, authoritative safety content with a named-and-answered misconception suits a pre-authored tap-to-reveal scene, where the sunglasses flap lets the child's own 'but I've got sunglasses' objection be surfaced and corrected rather than drifting toward 'so when IS it okay?'. The animated reveal is intended to make the simple mechanism (light gathering to a point inside the eye) more concrete for young learners without requiring them to master the optics; this is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: recognise that light from the sun can be dangerous and that there are ways to protect their eyes; non-statutory guidance warns pupils that it is not safe to look directly at the sun, even when wearing dark glasses.

Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.
learnerActions: Look at an illustration of a child outdoors under the Sun and predict aloud or in writing: 'Is it ever safe to look straight at the Sun?'
Reveal the Sun-to-eye path: light gathers through the eye's lens to a tiny point inside the eye — caption 'the Sun can damage the inside of your eye for ever — never look straight at it.'
Reveal the sunglasses flap after stating your own thought 'but I've got sunglasses': 'sunglasses dim the brightness and block some UV — but they do NOT make it safe to stare at the Sun.'
Reveal the cloud: 'still not safe on a cloudy day — the Sun is still dangerously bright through thin cloud or haze.'

Reveal the pinhole/box projector: the safe way to watch the Sun is by looking at its projected image on a surface, never at the Sun itself and never by holding anything up to your eyes toward the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Looking directly at the Sun is never safe, and the common reasons children think it becomes safe — such as wearing sunglasses or the Sun looking dim behind cloud — are each wrong; there is a separate safe way to observe the Sun indirectly.

activities.title: UV-bead fair test: which sunglasses block the most UV?
feedback: Praise a controlled comparison: if the beads started uncoloured, matched, and were in the same light at the same time, with only the sunglasses changed, then differences in the beads are fair evidence about UV blocking.
If a learner concludes the best UV-blocking glasses make it safe to stare: separate 'protects your eyes generally' from 'lets you look at the Sun' — the rule to never look directly still holds.
Reminder for the outdoor set-up: observe the beads on the ground or table, never look up at the Sun and never hold sunglasses up to your eyes toward the Sun to test them.
activities.rationale: A hands-on UV-bead comparison provides evidence for the 'ways to protect' half of the objective and is intended to give practice in fair-test reasoning, while the explicit caution prevents the dangerous over-extension from UV protection to safe direct viewing. This is a proposed supporting activity and must never let a child experience looking at the Sun.
sourceClaims: Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.
learnerActions: Set out UV-sensitive beads and watch THE BEADS change colour in sunlight (or a UV source) — keep your eyes on the beads, never on the Sun.

Using fresh beads that have been kept out of sunlight (not the beads already coloured in the first step), put a matching set of beads under each pair of sunglasses (or under clear plastic spread with sun cream), plus one uncovered set to compare. Lay them out side by side in the same light at the same time, keeping everything else the same, and observe how much each set changes colour.
Record which item lets the beads change least, i.e. which blocks the most UV, and discuss what makes this a fair test (same beads, same light, change only the sunglasses).
State explicitly: blocking the most UV is NOT the same as making it safe to look straight at the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: There are testable, evidence-based 'ways to protect' — the test can show whether some sunglasses block more UV than others (and how dark a lens looks does not tell you how much UV it blocks) — but blocking UV helps protect eyes from UV exposure and does not permit staring at the Sun.

activities.title: Eyes vs skin: sorting protections and checking the rule
feedback: If a learner equates the Sun with a lamp: the Sun is vastly more intense than ordinary household lamps and, unlike them, can cause permanent eye damage — so never look directly at it.
If a learner tries to place 'shade' in only one group: shade legitimately protects both eyes and skin, so it belongs in both.
Reinforce that everyone, of every skin tone, needs UV protection.
activities.rationale: Categorising and short rule-checks reinforce and assess the safety knowledge and the eyes-vs-skin distinction. A sort-and-check task can confirm the rule and vocabulary but does not by itself require the learner to construct the reasoning aloud, so it is paired with the spoken explanation prompts for the cloudy-day and torch cases.
sourceClaims: Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.
learnerActions: Sort protection actions into 'protects eyes' (sunglasses, never staring, safe indirect viewing) and 'protects skin' (sunscreen, clothing); note that 'shade' and 'a sun hat' are shared items that belong in BOTH groups, so this sort allows an item to go in two places.
Answer short check questions: Is it safe to look at the Sun while wearing sunglasses? (No.) Is it safe on a cloudy day? (No.)
State the rule in your own words and give one simple reason, then name at least two ways to protect your eyes outside on a very bright day.
Discuss the torch question: why is a quick glance at a torch different from a glance at the Sun?
activities.intendedInsight: Eye protection and skin protection meet different needs (with shade and a sun hat helping both); the Sun is far more intense than any ordinary household light, so we must never look directly at it, whereas a quick accidental glance at an ordinary torch is unlikely to harm your eyes (though we still should not stare into torches).

activities.title: Ask the eye doctor: why can't I look at the Sun?
feedback: Keep the message fixed: the answer is always 'never look directly, even with sunglasses' — do not negotiate exceptions.
If instruments come up: binoculars and telescopes concentrate the Sun's light and make direct viewing far more dangerous, never safer.
activities.rationale: A role-play with an authoritative persona may be engaging and may motivate the 'why'; because the message is a non-negotiable safety rule for young children, any dialogue should deliver the fixed answer and avoid open-ended drift toward exceptions, so keep it tightly scripted or use it after the rule is secure. The persona's core 'never, even with sunglasses' message is supported by the curriculum/misconception sources; the 'instruments make it worse' detail rests on the Ogden Trust source, which is marked unverified in the row.
sourceClaims: Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.

The eye's lens is about four times as powerful as a magnifying glass and focuses sunlight to a point on the retina that can burn the light-sensitive cells and cause permanent damage; the effect is worse through unfiltered cameras/telescopes/binoculars; safe observation uses indirect methods such as projection.
learnerActions: Pose a child's questions to an optometrist/eye-doctor persona: 'Why can't I look at the Sun?' and 'What if I wear sunglasses?'

Hear the authoritative answer: the Sun is so intensely bright it can permanently damage the light-sensitive cells inside the eye; sunglasses reduce glare but do not make looking safe; instruments like binoculars or telescopes make it far worse.
Repeat the rule back in your own words and name the safe indirect way to watch the Sun (looking at its projected image on a surface, never directly).
activities.intendedInsight: An expert confirms the same single rule and reason, reinforcing that there are no exceptions and that instruments increase the danger.

constraints: The load-bearing outcome is a non-negotiable safety rule plus a simple reason: NEVER look directly at the Sun, even with dark glasses, even on a cloudy day — because it can permanently damage the eyes.

No activity may ever invite, simulate, or rehearse a child looking directly at the Sun, nor ask whether a child can see the Sun through a cover or hold any material up to the eyes toward the Sun; provide only safe indirect viewing (a pinhole/box projector that shows a projected image on a surface, or observing UV beads on the ground/table).
Blocking UV (by sunglasses or sun cream) is not the same as making direct viewing safe; keep 'protects your eyes generally' separate from 'lets you stare at the Sun' whenever UV testing is discussed.

The optics of the lens focusing light onto the retina is teacher background to justify the rule, not a pupil expectation; pupils are expected to state the rule, give a simple reason, and name protections. The Ogden Trust 'four times a magnifying glass' figure is unverified and is teacher background only, never a pupil-facing fact.

A sort-and-check task can confirm the rule and vocabulary but does not by itself elicit independent spoken/written explanation; pair it with prompts that ask learners to explain the cloudy-day and torch cases in their own words.
Model accurate language ('the Sun appears to move across the sky') to avoid seeding Sun/Earth astronomy misconceptions, and state that all skin tones need UV protection.
This is a statutory objective in the England national curriculum Year 3 science programme (Light unit); it has no direct NGSS performance-expectation equivalent.
Shade is a protection that helps both eyes and skin; where protections are sorted, allow it to belong to both groups.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles or delivered content, not the efficacy of any specific activity or format.

The Ogden Trust claim (lens ~four times a magnifying glass; worse through cameras/telescopes/binoculars; indirect projection is safe) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the quantitative 'four times' detail as teacher background only and do not present it to pupils as a fact to learn. The broad 'instruments make direct viewing worse' caution is retained as a safety-positive message, but its specific source is unverified.

No source directly supports the persona/role-play pedagogy as such; the Ogden and misconception claims cited on that activity support the delivered factual content and the fixed safety message, not a claim that a persona format is more effective than another medium.

The row's claim that a 3D or open-dialogue format would 'dramatise' or risk rehearsing looking at the Sun is a design caution, not an established comparative fact; it is reframed here as a narrowly scoped safety constraint (no activity should simulate direct Sun-gazing) rather than a universal law about media.
Legacy confidence was recorded as 'high'; this rewrite does not independently re-verify that rating.

probeDeeper: Name two ways to protect your eyes outside on a very bright, sunny day.
A torch and the sun are both light sources — why is it OK to glance at a torch but never at the sun?
It's cloudy and the sun looks dim behind the clouds — is it safe to look straight at it now? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Sunglasses cut down brightness and glare, but they do NOT make it safe to look straight at the sun — you should never look directly at it, because the sun is so intensely bright it can permanently damage your eyes even through sunglasses. Protect your eyes with shade, a hat, and by not looking at it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Protection equals permission: 'sunglasses (or squinting) make it safe to look right at the sun'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sunglasses reduce glare for comfort but never make direct sun-gazing safe; the safe move is not to look at all. Separate 'protects your eyes generally' from 'lets you stare at the sun'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — dark sunglasses make it safe to look right at the sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes — sunglasses make direct looking safe

errorPatterns.pattern: Dimness equals safe: 'on a cloudy or hazy day, or at sunset, you can look at the sun'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The sun is still dangerously bright through thin cloud or haze; don't judge safety by how bright it happens to look.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's fine to look at the sun when it's cloudy or the sun looks dim.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a cloudy/hazy day or a low, dim-looking sun is safe to look at

errorPatterns.pattern: Sun is just a big lamp: 'you can glance at a torch, so a quick look at the sun is OK too'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The sun is vastly more intense than any artificial light and, unlike them, can cause permanent damage — even a brief direct look is unsafe.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates the sun with household lights; thinks a brief glance is harmless

responseLevels.gap: Thinks sunglasses, squinting, cloud, or a dim-looking sun make it safe to look directly at the sun, or treats the sun like an ordinary lamp.
responseLevels.full: States that looking directly at the sun is never safe and can permanently damage eyes; that sunglasses/hat/shade reduce brightness but don't permit staring; and explains the sun is far more intense than artificial light — transferring to the cloudy-day and torch cases.
responseLevels.partial: Knows you shouldn't stare at the sun and can name a protection, but still believes some condition (sunglasses, cloud) makes direct looking safe.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your friend puts on dark sunglasses and says 'Now it's safe for me to look straight at the sun.' Is your friend right? Explain what you would tell them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Children know sunglasses 'protect' their eyes, so they over-extend that to 'sunglasses make the sun safe to stare at'. The prompt forces the decision of whether protection equals permission to look. A child with the concept refuses to look directly even with sunglasses; a child without it treats protection as a green light.
